title: San Martin Steps Aside at Guayaquil
text:
By 1822 Jose de San Martin had led an army across the Andes, freed Chile and taken Lima, where he ruled as Protector of Peru. But Spanish armies still held the Peruvian highlands, and his forces were not strong enough to finish the war alone. In the north, Simon Bolivar had freed Venezuela, Colombia and now Ecuador.

The two liberators met at Guayaquil, in what is now Ecuador, on July 26 and 27, 1822. They talked in private and no record of the conversation was kept. Historians believe San Martin hoped for military help and that the two men disagreed about the future form of government, Bolivar favoring a republic and San Martin a constitutional monarchy.

Whatever was said, San Martin drew his own conclusion. He returned to Lima, and on September 20, 1822, before the first Congress of Peru, he resigned all his powers. He left Peru that night, went to Chile and Argentina, and later to Europe, where he lived quietly for the rest of his life. Bolivar's armies completed the liberation of Peru in 1824.
lesson: Sometimes the best thing a leader can do for the cause is to step aside so that someone else can finish it.
people: Jose de San Martin, Simon Bolivar
source: San Martin's letters and proclamation on leaving Peru; standard histories of South American independence
caveat: What was said at Guayaquil is unknown, and a letter attributed to San Martin explaining his reasons is of disputed authenticity.
